newsitem.title: UK: Gold steadier after sell-off, but more losses seen.
newsitem.headline: Gold steadier after sell-off, but more losses seen.

text.p: Gold steadied around $341.50 an ounce after Monday's late pounding by funds shaved $5 off prices, but further losses were seen on the horizon.

Gold's failure to bounce from $345 was seen as critical and heralding a move to the February 12 low of $336.15, which was the lowest since April 1993. But the market might consolidate first, dealers said.
"It will make a new low below $336 and maybe it will find a base somewhere above $300," said one London dealer.
Dealers said a combination of factors, such as negative charts, expected interest rate hikes in the U.S. and continued producer selling, might have turned funds sour on gold.
Bullion fixed $1.55 lower at $341.45 an ounce on Wednesday and against New York's close of $341.80/$342.30.
The sharp fall started on Friday as higher U.S. producer price inflation pointed to interest rate rises. Tuesday's lower-than-forecast U.S. consumer price rises added fuel to the decline.
Brokers GNI said just about everything was negative news for gold at the moment. "Negative action on any news is the best confirmation of a bear market that you can get," it said.
Others said a rise of a few basis points in inflation might not be a good reason to buy gold, and higher interest rates were a reason to sell.
Dealers noted strong physical demand, particularly out of the Middle East, and the market could consolidate before probing lower. But funds were likely to have more gold to dump.
"I think the market is pretty sanguine about it. We have seen good selling, particularly out of the funds, and we don't think the funds will let go for a while," said another dealer.
"A day or two of consolidation is likely to stall out under $343.60-$343.70, and give way to a final proble lower," said analyst Peter Rehmer of Elliott Wave International.
Silver held steady at $4.72/$4.74 after emerging from the assault on gold almost unscathed.
Dealers saw no reason to sell silver at the moment after the market fell 70 cents from the March peak.
"It would need some help from gold to fire it but it won't necessarily move lower on the back of gold," said one dealer.
Platinum was heading down to the lower end of its range at $360 which, if broken, might send prices down towards $350.
But it was quoted up $1.50 at $364.50/$365.50 on Wednesday.
Palladium shed $1.20 to $149.00/$150.00 as traders awaited news on delayed Russian shipments to leading importer Japan.
"Palladium is dependent on what shipments are genuinely coming out," said one. But lease rates were still tight.
